title: Historia Regum Britanniae
alternative_titles: The History of the Kings of Britain
description: Pseudohistorical chronicle tracing the kings of Britain from the legendary Brutus of Troy to the Saxon conquest, the principal source of the Arthurian legend in England. Geoffrey claims to translate 'a certain very ancient book in the British tongue' given him by Walter, archdeacon of Oxford; its authority was attacked by William of Newburgh and Gerald of Wales but it decisively shaped medieval British historiography.
summary: Geoffrey of Monmouth narrates the foundation of Britain by Brutus, a descendant of Aeneas, and proceeds through the reigns of the legendary kings — Lear, Cymbeline, and above all Arthur, whose conquests extend over much of Europe — to the Saxon domination and the prophecies of Merlin (the Prophetiae Merlini, later incorporated as Book VII). The work made Arthur a pan-European figure and provided the framework for Wace, Layamon, and the later chronicle tradition.
significance: The single most influential piece of British historical writing of the Middle Ages: over 200 manuscripts survive, and it furnished the matter of Britain for romance, chronicle, and national myth from Wace's Roman de Brut to Malory and beyond.
provenance_and_manuscripts: Over 200 manuscripts, the earliest from the twelfth century (e.g., Bern, Burgerbibliothek MS 568, c. 1200); dedicated, in variant prologues, to Robert, earl of Gloucester, Waleran, count of Meulan, and King Stephen.
editions: The History of the Kings of Britain, ed. Michael D. Reeve, trans. Neil Wright (Woodbridge: Boydell Press, 2007)
modern_translations: Lewis Thorpe, The History of the Kings of Britain (London: Penguin, 1966)
research_notes: Composition dated c. 1136–38 from the completion of the Historia by Henry of Huntingdon's own account and the dedication variants. Not to be confused with the later French and English vernacular adaptations.

title: Gesta Regum Anglorum
alternative_titles: Deeds of the Kings of the English
description: William of Malmesbury's history of the English kings from the arrival of the Anglo-Saxons (449) to the twenty-eighth year of Henry I (1127–28), the most learned English history of the twelfth century, deliberately modelled on Bede and written with a polished Latinity that set a new standard for English historiography.
summary: Five books carry the narrative from the adventus Saxonum through the kings of Wessex and the Norman Conquest to Henry I; the work combines narrative history with biography, anecdote, and documentary research, drawing on a library of sources now partly lost and on William's own travels and enquiries.
significance: The outstanding English historical work between Bede and the later twelfth century; a model of critical method and style, cited and pillaged by later chroniclers, and a primary witness to Anglo-Saxon history after the Conquest.
provenance_and_manuscripts: Survives in four recensions representing successive authorial revisions (c. 1126, c. 1135, and later additions); earliest manuscripts from the twelfth century.
editions: Gesta Regum Anglorum, ed. and trans. R. A. B. Mynors, R. M. Thomson, and M. Winterbottom, 2 vols (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1998–99)
modern_translations: J. A. Giles, William of Malmesbury's Chronicle of the Kings of England (London, 1847)
research_notes: The Gesta Pontificum Anglorum (1125) and Historia Novella (c. 1141) are companion works by the same author; only the Gesta Regum is entered here to avoid fragmenting the record.

title: Historia Anglorum
description: Henry of Huntingdon's history of England from the earliest times to the accession of Henry II in 1154, notable for its vivid battle narratives, its interest in the English past as national history, and the substantial body of original verse — including the political poems addressed to Henry I — embedded in the prose.
summary: Ten books (the latest recension) move from Roman and Anglo-Saxon Britain through the Norman kings to the anarchy of Stephen's reign; the work incorporates earlier sources (Bede, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle) while supplying independent contemporary witness for the twelfth century, including the famous account of the Battle of Lincoln.
significance: A principal narrative source for the reign of Stephen, and a central text of twelfth-century English national historiography; its verse makes it a bridge between Anglo-Latin and vernacular literary traditions.
provenance_and_manuscripts: Over 30 manuscripts in successive authorial recensions (ending 1129, 1135, 1138, 1148, and 1154); autograph revisions survive in later copies.
editions: Henry, Archdeacon of Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum: The History of the English People, ed. and trans. Diana Greenway (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1996)
modern_translations: Diana Greenway, The History of the English People 1000–1154 (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2002)
research_notes: The work circulated under varying titles; Greenway's edition is the standard. The six-book version ended in 1135; the final recension extends to 1154.

title: Itinerarium Cambriae
description: Gerald of Wales's account of the preaching tour of Wales undertaken in 1188 with Archbishop Baldwin of Canterbury to recruit for the Third Crusade, combining topographical description, ethnography of the Welsh, anecdote, and vigorous self-promotion; the companion work to the Descriptio Cambriae (1194).
summary: Gerald narrates the itinerary of Baldwin's mission through south and north Wales, recording the sermons, the reception of the party, local marvels and legends, the character and customs of the Welsh, and his own prominent role in the enterprise; the two books culminate in the preaching of the cross.
significance: One of the finest works of twelfth-century travel and ethnographic writing, a primary source for medieval Wales, and a major witness to the Latin literary culture of the Welsh marches.
provenance_and_manuscripts: Survives in a small number of medieval manuscripts; first printed 1585 (London).
editions: Giraldi Cambrensis Opera, vol. VI: Itinerarium Kambriae et Descriptio Kambriae, ed. James F. Dimock, Rolls Series 21 (London, 1868)
modern_translations: Lewis Thorpe, The Journey Through Wales and The Description of Wales (London: Penguin, 1978)
research_notes: The Descriptio Cambriae is treated in scholarship as the companion piece; only the Itinerarium is entered as a separate record here.

title: Expugnatio Hibernica
description: Gerald of Wales's history of the Anglo-Norman invasion and conquest of Ireland (1169–85), framed as a panegyric of Henry II and of Gerald's own relatives among the conquerors, the Geraldines; composed from 1188 and read publicly at Oxford in 1188 or 1189.
summary: Gerald recounts the coming of the Normans under Strongbow and the campaigns that established English lordship in Ireland, devoting special attention to the deeds of the FitzGeralds, to the character of the Irish, and to the prophecies and prodigies attending the conquest.
significance: The foundational narrative of the English presence in Ireland, shaped by family partisanship but indispensable as the earliest extended account of the conquest; a model of twelfth-century historical rhetoric.
provenance_and_manuscripts: Over 20 manuscripts; the work exists in an earlier and a later authorial recension.
editions: Giraldi Cambrensis Opera, vol. V: Expugnatio Hibernica, ed. James F. Dimock, Rolls Series 21 (London, 1867)
modern_translations: A. B. Scott and F. X. Martin, Expugnatio Hibernica: The Conquest of Ireland (Dublin: Royal Irish Academy, 1978)
research_notes: The Topographia Hibernica (c. 1188) preceded and complements it; only the Expugnatio is entered separately here.

title: De Nugis Curialium
description: Walter Map's miscellany of court gossip, satire, Welsh legend, ghost story, and moral anecdote, assembled piecemeal during his service at the court of Henry II; 'a jest book and a jest at the same time', as one editor put it, and the only certain work by one of the wittiest Latin writers of the age.
summary: Five distinctiones gather tales of the court of Henry II, satirical portraits of monks and courtiers, the legend of Sadius and Galo, the story of the Welsh king Herla and the fairy bride, and the earliest surviving connected account of the birth of Lancelot; Map's dissuasio to his friend Ruffinus against marriage closes the work.
significance: A unique window onto the oral culture and court life of Henry II's England, an early witness to Arthurian material, and a masterpiece of twelfth-century Latin satire and narrative.
provenance_and_manuscripts: Survives in a single manuscript: Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Bodley 851 (late twelfth or early thirteenth century).
editions: De Nugis Curialium: Courtiers' Trifles, ed. and trans. M. R. James, rev. C. N. L. Brooke and R. A. B. Mynors (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1983)
modern_translations: Frederick Tupper and Marbury Bladen Ogle, Master Walter Map's Book (London: Chatto & Windus, 1924)
research_notes: Ascribed works on the Lancelot prose cycle are now discounted. Composition spans c. 1181–92; the Bodley manuscript preserves the work in a disordered state.

title: Policraticus
alternative_titles: Policraticus: Of the Frivolities of Courtiers and the Footprints of Philosophers
description: John of Salisbury's treatise on politics, court life, and philosophy in eight books, completed in 1159 and dedicated to Thomas Becket; the first full work of medieval political theory, famous for its organic metaphor of the body politic and its defence of tyrannicide.
summary: The Policraticus satirizes the frivolities of courtiers, expounds the duties of prince and magistrate under the image of the body politic (the prince as head, the clergy as soul), argues that the tyrant is a public enemy whose killing may be lawful, and ends with a survey of ancient philosophy and the true happiness of the contemplative life.
significance: The most important political treatise written in twelfth-century Europe, a conduit of classical political thought into the Middle Ages, and a standard authority cited into the seventeenth century.
provenance_and_manuscripts: Over 60 manuscripts survive, with early copies from the twelfth century onward.
editions: Ioannis Saresberiensis Policraticus I–IV, ed. K. S. B. Keats-Rohan, Corpus Christianorum Continuatio Mediaevalis 118 (Turnhout: Brepols, 1993)
modern_translations: Cary J. Nederman, John of Salisbury: Policraticus (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990)
John Dickinson, The Statesman's Book of John of Salisbury (New York: Knopf, 1927)
research_notes: The companion Metalogicon (1159), a defence of the trivium, is not entered separately here. The Metalogicon and Policraticus form a designed pair.

title: Chronica Majora
description: Matthew Paris's universal and English chronicle, revised and expanded from Roger of Wendover's Flores Historiarum and continued by Matthew with his own annals down to 1259; the greatest historical work of thirteenth-century England, illustrated with Matthew's own marginal drawings.
summary: Beginning with the creation, the Chronica Majora concentrates on English and European affairs from the Norman Conquest onward, becoming a detailed contemporary record for the reign of Henry III: the conflicts with the barons, the campaigns in Wales and Gascony, the affairs of the friars and the universities, and the author's outspoken criticisms of king and pope.
significance: The fullest and most vivid narrative source for thirteenth-century England, and a landmark of English book production through its author's maps and marginal illustrations.
provenance_and_manuscripts: Three principal authorial manuscripts: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MSS 26 and 16, and London, British Library, MS Royal 14 C. vii (the latter with maps and illustrations).
editions: Matthaei Parisiensis Chronica Majora, ed. Henry Richards Luard, 7 vols, Rolls Series 57 (London, 1872–83)
modern_translations: J. A. Giles, Matthew Paris's English History, 3 vols (London, 1852–54)
manuscript_locations: London, British Library, MS Royal 14 C. vii
research_notes: Matthew's own abridgement, the Historia Anglorum (c. 1250–55), is a separate work and is not entered here to avoid confusion with Henry of Huntingdon's work of the same title.

title: Philobiblon
description: Richard de Bury's treatise in praise of books and of the love of learning, completed on his birthday, 24 January 1345 (i.e., 1344 by modern reckoning), while he was bishop of Durham; the work draws on his experience assembling one of the great private libraries of medieval England.
summary: In twenty chapters the Philobiblon celebrates the wisdom preserved in books, argues that they should be shared with scholars rather than hoarded, defends the clergy against the charge of neglecting their books, and prescribes the care, repair, and circulation of manuscripts; it closes with provisions for the dispersal of the author's own library to the scholars of Oxford.
significance: The most famous medieval book about books, a primary witness to the book culture of fourteenth-century England, and a key document for the history of libraries and of Oxford scholarship.
provenance_and_manuscripts: Over 30 manuscripts survive, the earliest from the fourteenth century; traditionally dated 1344 (completed 24 January 1345).
editions: The Philobiblon of Richard de Bury, ed. and trans. Michael Maclagan (Oxford: Basil Blackwell, 1960)
modern_translations: E. C. Thomas, The Love of Books: The Philobiblon of Richard de Bury (London: Alexander Moring, 1903)
Ernest C. Thomas, ed. Michael Maclagan, Philobiblon (Oxford: Blackwell, 1960)
research_notes: The work's authorship has been discussed (some scholarship attributes drafting to Robert Holcot), but Richard de Bury remains the accepted author. Modern editions correct the calendar date of completion.

title: Opus Maius
description: Roger Bacon's encyclopedic proposal for the reform of learning, written c. 1267 at the request of Pope Clement IV and sent to him with the Opus Minus and Opus Tertium; its seventh part on moral philosophy and its treatment of optics, experimental science, and the applications of mathematics to theology make it a landmark of thirteenth-century thought.
summary: Bacon surveys the causes of error, the relation of philosophy to scripture, the utility of grammar and of the learned languages (Hebrew, Greek, Arabic), mathematics and its uses (including calendar reform and geography), the science of perspective, experimental science, and moral philosophy — arguing throughout that the sciences are necessary instruments for the understanding and defence of the faith.
significance: The fullest medieval statement of an experimental and mathematically grounded program of learning; a foundation text for the later reputation of Bacon and a principal witness to thirteenth-century optics and natural philosophy.
provenance_and_manuscripts: Over 20 manuscripts; the Opus Minus and Opus Tertium, which abbreviate and supplement it, survive in fewer copies.
editions: The 'Opus Majus' of Roger Bacon, ed. John Henry Bridges, 3 vols (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1897–1900)
modern_translations: Robert Belle Burke, The Opus Majus of Roger Bacon, 2 vols (Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 1928)
research_notes: Composed rapidly in 1266–67 following the papal mandate of 1266; the Opus Minus and Opus Tertium are treated here as companion pieces rather than separate records.

title: Ordinatio
description: Duns Scotus's great revision of his Oxford lectures on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, left unfinished at his death; the Ordinatio sets out the subtle doctor's metaphysics of univocity, his formal distinction, his defence of the Immaculate Conception, and his voluntarist ethics, and became the authoritative alternative to Thomism in late medieval theology.
summary: In four books following the structure of the Sentences, Scotus develops a systematic theology distinguished by its precise use of logic: the univocal concept of being, the formal distinction, the primacy of the will, the demonstration of God's existence through the concept of infinite being, and the case for Mary's immaculate conception — arguments that set the agenda for fourteenth-century scholasticism.
significance: One of the most demanding and influential works of medieval philosophy and theology; the foundation of the Scotist school, taught in the universities into the seventeenth century and beyond.
provenance_and_manuscripts: Left incomplete; transmitted with the earlier Lectura and reportationes of the Oxford lectures; the standard modern text is the Vatican critical edition (1950– ).
editions: Ioannis Duns Scoti Opera Omnia, ed. Commissio Scotistica (Vatican City: Typis Polyglottis Vaticanis, 1950– )
modern_translations: Allan B. Wolter, Duns Scotus: Philosophical Writings (Indianapolis: Hackett, 1987) [selections]
research_notes: Dates follow the consensus that the Oxford lectures began c. 1300 and the Ordinatio was composed in stages before Scotus's transfer to Paris (1302) and after his return; the work was left incomplete at his death in 1308.

title: Summa Logicae
description: William of Ockham's systematic treatise on logic, written c. 1323 before his summons to Avignon; in three parts it expounds terms, propositions, and the theory of argument, developing the nominalist ontology — the rejection of universals as real entities — for which Ockham is chiefly remembered.
summary: Part I analyses terms and the problem of universals, arguing that only individuals exist and that universal concepts are signs in the mind; Part II treats propositions and the properties of terms; Part III examines syllogistic, demonstrative, and probable argument, including the analysis of fallacies. The work is the vehicle of Ockham's razor in its methodological form: entities are not to be multiplied without necessity.
significance: The most influential logic textbook of the later Middle Ages; its nominalism reshaped fourteenth-century philosophy and theology and remains a principal point of reference in the history of logic.
provenance_and_manuscripts: Survives in many manuscripts; standard modern editions in the Opera Philosophica et Theologica (1967–88).
editions: Guillelmi de Ockham Summa Logicae, ed. Philotheus Boehner, Gedeon Gál, and Stephen F. Brown, Opera Philosophica 1 (St Bonaventure, NY: Franciscan Institute, 1974)
modern_translations: Michael J. Loux, Ockham's Theory of Terms: Part I of the Summa Logicae (Notre Dame: University of Notre Dame Press, 1974)
research_notes: The work circulated in a later revised version; the standard dating places the original composition c. 1323, with revision continuing into Ockham's Avignon period.
